A sample almost never arrives at the tempo and key of your track. There are two ways to change it.

## Repitch: speed and pitch together

Play a record faster and it gets higher; slower and it gets lower. That is **repitching**. A turntable's pitch fader does it, and so do
the classic samplers (the E-mu SP-1200, the Akai MPC60, the SP-404's pitch knob).

- Twice as fast = one **octave** up (12 semitones). Half speed = an octave down.
- One semitone is a speed change of about **5.95 %** (the twelfth root of two is 1.0595).
- So a turntable's **±8 %** pitch range is about ±1.3 semitones; **±16 %** about ±2.6.

Repitching keeps transients sharp and sounds natural, because nothing is invented: it is the same sound, faster or slower. Pitching
soul vocals up gave the "chipmunk soul" sound of early-2000s hip-hop; slowing whole songs down is the Houston "chopped and screwed" style.

## Time-stretch: apart

**Time-stretching** changes the length without changing the pitch (and **pitch-shifting** the pitch without the length). The computer
cuts the sound into tiny overlapping grains and spaces them further apart or closer together. Done simply, you hear it: drums smear,
a "phasey" or metallic sound appears. Modern algorithms (Ableton Live's Warp modes, élastique in many DAWs, DJ software's key lock) hide
it much better, but stretch anything far enough and it shows.

## Hear the difference

<div class="sp-pads" data-id="sp-pitch" data-loop="demo:soul84" data-slice="beats" data-show="wave pads edit library"></div>

1. Pick pad 1 (a chord). Set **Pitch** to +5 in **Repitch** mode. Shorter and higher, like a sped-up record.
2. Change **Mode** to **Stretch**. The same +5 semitones, but the chord keeps its length.
3. Leave pitch at 0 and set **Length** to ×2 in each mode. Repitch: an octave down and twice as long. Stretch: same pitch, twice as long,
   and listen to the attack: blurred. This sampler uses plain overlap-add on purpose, so the smear is easy to hear.
4. Load the **Funky Break**, slice **At the hits**, and stretch a snare to ×1.5 in each mode. Which would you put in a track?

## Matching a sample to your track

The arithmetic: the speed you need is **your tempo ÷ the sample's tempo**. A 90 BPM break in a 100 BPM track: 100 ÷ 90 = 1.111, so 11.1 %
faster, which repitched is about +1.8 semitones. If the key matters, choose:

- **Repitch** to the nearest key and adjust the track's tempo to fit (producers often build the track at the sample's speed), or
- **Stretch** to the exact tempo and pitch-shift separately, accepting some artefacts.

## The DJ's version: pitch fader and key lock

On a turntable the pitch fader is repitch. Below, push deck A's fader to +8 %: BPM and key both move; the readout shows the shift in
semitones. DJ software and CDJs add **key lock** (Master Tempo on Pioneer gear): tempo changes, pitch stays, by time-stretching.

## Many samples, one instrument

Pitch a single note far and it stops sounding like the instrument. A real instrument's body resonates at the same frequencies whatever
note is played, but a repitched sample moves those resonances with the note: a piano sample shifted up an octave sounds small and
"chipmunked", shifted down it sounds slow and woolly. So sampled instruments are built from **many recordings** (a **multi-sample**):

- **Key zones.** A note recorded every few semitones (often every minor third), each covering the keys around it, so no note is pitched far.
- **Velocity layers.** The same note recorded soft and hard. A hard hit isn't just louder: it's brighter, with more attack. Turning a
  soft recording up doesn't make it sound hard.
- **Round robin.** Several takes of each note and layer, played in turn. Repeat one recording and you hear the **machine-gun effect**,
  the same hit every time.

Choose **Multi-sample** in the sampler's menu. The demo is a plucked string recorded at C2, C3, C4 and C5, soft and hard, three takes each
(24 recordings). The map has keys across and velocity up; each coloured block is a zone.

<div class="sp-pads" data-id="sp-multi" data-kind="multi"></div>

1. Click across the bottom of the map, then across the top. The top uses the hard layer: brighter, with a knock.
2. Click the same spot again and again, then untick **Round robin**. Now every hit is the same take.
3. Tick **One sample only** and play from C2 up to C6. Every key now comes from the C4 recording. Low notes go dull and slow, high
   ones thin. That's why instruments are sampled every few notes.
4. With your own recordings: name each file with its note (and, if you have them, a layer and a take), e.g. `Guitar_E2_soft_rr1.wav`,
   then **Load recordings…**. **Spread zones** fills the keyboard between them.

In other gear this is a sampler instrument: Ableton's **Sampler** (Zone editor), Logic's **Sampler** (Mapping pane), Kontakt, and the
SFZ and SoundFont file formats. On an MPC it's a **keygroup** program.
